paras: The Bisbee clash between police and Tenth Cavalry troopers was a street fight in Bisbee, Arizona, on the night of July 3-4, 1919, in which city police and white civilians tried to disarm Black soldiers of the 10th U.S. Cavalry who had come to town for the Fourth of July parade. Five people were reported wounded, among them three troopers and a white deputy sheriff, and fourteen soldiers were arrested and handed over to the military authorities. Black papers in Chicago, Baltimore, Dallas and Phoenix carried the story, blaming a white military policeman's insult or the police.

The troopers came over from Fort Huachuca under Col. George B. White to take part in Bisbee's Fourth of July parade. According to the Phoenix Tribune's Bisbee correspondent, Myrtle Treat, a few soldiers of the Tenth arrived on July 3, tired after riding through the hot sun.

The wire account traced the fight to George Sullivan, a military policeman of the 19th Cavalry, whom the Defender identified as white. In the Whip's telling, Sullivan cursed a passing trooper, who struck him over both eyes and began taking his arms, whereupon watching white civilians and police joined in on Sullivan's side. The Defender's version said Sullivan, after using profane language, tried to draw his pistol and was overpowered and beaten, 'it is claimed'.

The troopers then refused to give up their weapons at their officers' request; the Afro-American wrote that they knew they would be at the mercy of the white M.P.s. A general alarm went out to disarm all Black men, and in the course of the disarming about a hundred shots were exchanged. The wounded were named as Deputy Sheriff Joseph Hardwick (spelled 'Josefus' in the Whip), a Mexican woman and three troopers.

Fourteen troopers were arrested and turned over to the military authorities. At the mayor's request, troops of the First Cavalry, which the Defender described as white, came from Douglas to help the military and city police prevent further trouble. The Defender reported that a court-martial had been ordered, though no report of its outcome appears in the coverage. The troopers did take part in the parade and field events, Treat wrote, but were not allowed out of their camp otherwise.

The Chicago Whip ran the story first, on July 9, under the headline 'Pistol Shots Exchanged Following Insult' and a Bisbee dateline of July 7. Its writer retold the wire story as a stage play, calling the trooper 'the abused soldier' and describing police and civilians as onlookers who 'decided to become actors in behalf of Sullivan'. Two days later the Baltimore Afro-American's special dispatch ran under 'Regiment That Saved Roosevelt resents insult of white Policeman and Beats Him Severely' and said a repetition of the 'Houston Uprising' had been narrowly averted.

On July 12 the Chicago Defender put a Continental Press version on its front page as 'Five Wounded When Troops and Citizens Clash in Street Fight; Over 100 Shots Fired', while the Dallas Express printed the wire on page four, calling the troopers 'negro' throughout. The Defender's text added that 'the injustices assumed such large proportions that the troops revolted'.

The sharpest comment came from Treat, who asked why police had not asked the Tenth's commanding officer to disarm his men, as with white soldiers, and wrote that 'these were black men and the city officers thought to handle the matter themselves'. She called the episode 'a sample of the "democracy" for which our boys have been fighting'.

Accounts differ on who began the trouble: the wire and the Afro-American put the first insult on Sullivan, while Treat wrote that the police, trying to disarm the soldiers, began by beating several troopers and shooting into the group. The wire counted five wounded, the Phoenix Tribune four, one seriously, and the Afro-American two soldiers severely wounded.

The Defender's text says 'Fourteen of the 100 cavalrymen were killed', but the other three accounts say fourteen were arrested and none reports a death, so the word appears to be a misprint. The Whip's July 7 dateline would put the fight on the night of July 6, but the other papers date it July 4, and Treat's account of soldiers arriving July 3 and parading afterward supports the earlier date.

reader.title: Bisbee clash between police and Tenth Cavalry troopers (1919)
bases: City police, joined by white civilians, set out to disarm Black troopers of the 10th Cavalry, beating several and exchanging gunfire with them (A2, A3, A7, A8).

The wire story (A1-A3, A5-A7), the Afro-American's special dispatch (A4) and a local Bisbee correspondent (A8) agree on a clash in which police and civilians tried to disarm 10th Cavalry troopers and several people were wounded, though they differ on who started it.

accounts.label: Wire report (Whip, Defender, Dallas Express)
accounts.gist: A taunting or profane remark by MP George Sullivan led to a fight in which a trooper beat him; police and civilians joined in, the troopers refused to disarm, and about 100 shots were exchanged; five were wounded and fourteen troopers arrested.

accounts.label: Afro-American special dispatch
accounts.gist: A white MP's insult led to his being disarmed and beaten; the Tenth refused to disarm, fearing the white MPs; fourteen were arrested and two severely wounded, narrowly averting a 'Houston Uprising'.

accounts.label: Local Black correspondent (Phoenix Tribune)
accounts.gist: City police tried to disarm the newly arrived soldiers, beating several and shooting into the group; four were wounded, one seriously.

framing.detail: The Whip, under 'Pistol Shots Exchanged Following Insult', called the trooper 'the abused soldier' and mocked police and civilians as spectators who became 'actors in behalf of Sullivan'.
The Afro-American headlined 'Regiment That Saved Roosevelt resents insult of white Policeman and Beats Him Severely' and spoke of an averted repetition of the Houston uprising.
The Defender ran the Continental Press story, 'Five Wounded When Troops and Citizens Clash in Street Fight', adding 'it is claimed' and that injustices led the troops to revolt.
The Dallas Express printed the wire on page 4 as 'Negro Soldiers and Civilians Have Clash in Bisbee, Five Wounded'.
Myrtle Treat's Bisbee column blamed the police and called it 'a sample of the "democracy" for which our boys have been fighting'.
